problem: Earlier grounded-language systems had two failure modes. Some relied on hand-coded syntax and semantics, as SHRDLU did, and could not learn new concepts. Others learned only in highly structured or simplified environments. No agent had learned end-to-end to link words to raw pixels and long action sequences in a continuous 3D world. A plain RL agent in this setting does not learn at all from the sparse object-selection reward.
motivation: Instructing artificial agents at scale requires language understanding that is grounded in perception and action and learned rather than hand-coded. Early simulations showed that an A3C agent learning only from infrequent pick-up rewards learned nothing. This led the authors to exploit the dense perceptual stream through unsupervised auxiliary prediction objectives. They also study whether the grounded semantics generalise compositionally and speed up later word learning.
key_idea: An end-to-end actor-critic agent learns to follow templated text instructions in a 3D DeepMind Lab world. It combines the sparse reward signal with unsupervised auxiliary objectives: temporal autoencoding (next-frame prediction) and language prediction (predict the instruction word from vision). Curricula extend it to harder tasks.
insight: Grounded word learning in 3D depends on auxiliary unsupervised objectives. With RL alone the agent showed no learning after millions of episodes. It learned fastest with tAE and LP combined with reward prediction and value replay (Fig. 3). Much of early learning is 'pre-linguistic' visual-motor skill: an agent pre-trained on just 2 words learns a new 20-shape vocabulary much faster than one trained from scratch, and 20 pre-known words helps further, so word learning accelerates as knowledge grows. Generalisation to novel colour-shape bigrams emerges even when only bigrams are seen in training (decomposition/composition), and does so faster than with unigrams, because bigram episodes carry more information. 'larger/smaller' transfers almost perfectly to unseen shapes, whereas 'lighter/darker' transfers only above chance. Harder multi-room and multi-task settings are solvable only through curricula.
method: Vision module V: 3-layer CNN (8x8 stride 4 → 4x4 stride 2 → 3x3 stride 1) on 84x84 first-person RGB, output 64x7x7.
Language module L: word embeddings of dim 128, encoded by an LSTM (hidden 128) for word-order-sensitive tasks or a bag-of-words sum otherwise (faster training).

Mixing + action modules: flattened visual features concatenated with the language vector feed an LSTM action core (d=256; described as two-layer in the main text), whose state drives a softmax policy over discrete actions and a value head.
Training: Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) with 32 asynchronous workers, RMSProp, unroll length 50, action repeat 4, up to 640m steps.

Temporal autoencoder (tAE): predicts v_{t+1} from the conv encoding of v_t multiplicatively modulated by an action embedding (W_b a ⊙ W_v y), decoded with a deconv net under MSE loss. W_b is shared with the policy's final layer.

Language prediction (LP): the shared V encoder feeds a 128-d ReLU layer and then a softmax over the vocabulary, predicting an instruction word (NLL loss). Output weights are tied to L's word embeddings, which also makes the agent's perception interpretable.
Additional UNREAL auxiliaries (reward prediction RP, value replay VR) are used, and multi-lesson curricula handle complex layouts and multi-task (Selection / Next-to / In-room) learning.

setting.backbone: 3-layer CNN + LSTM/BOW language encoder + LSTM action core (trained from scratch with A3C + auxiliary losses)
setting.training_data: Procedurally generated DeepMind Lab levels (rooms with objects from 40 shapes × 13 colours × 9 patterns × 3 shades × 3 sizes, templated instructions). Reward-based RL, up to 640m environment steps, 16 hyperparameter replicas per condition, with curricula for complex tasks.
setting.action_space: discrete motor actions (movement/look/pick-up) with action repeat 4
setting.simulator: DeepMind Lab (extended with a language channel)

numbers_note: No numeric results tables. All results (auxiliary-objective ablation, word-learning speed, compositional/relational generalisation, curriculum and multi-task learning) are reported only as learning curves in figures on custom DeepMind Lab tasks. No standard navigation benchmark is used.
results: With pure RL (A3C) the agent learned nothing even after millions of episodes on a 59-word vocabulary task. Adding tAE + LP + RP + VR auxiliaries gave the fastest learning. The trained agent zero-shot interprets held-out colour-shape bigrams, including when trained only on bigrams. It applies 'larger/smaller' to unseen shapes almost perfectly and 'lighter/darker' to unseen colours above chance. Via curricula, a single agent learns room-conditioned retrieval and three multi-task instruction types (Selection, Next to, In room). Comparisons are only against its own ablations (RL-only and subsets of the auxiliary losses).
limitations: Synthetic, templated language with a small fixed vocabulary in simple object-retrieval tasks within toy DeepMind Lab rooms; no natural human instructions or realistic scenes.

Results are given only as learning curves (mean of best 5 of 16 hyperparameter replicas), with no standardized benchmark or quantitative tables. Harder tasks need hand-designed curricula to learn at all.
The LP objective requires extracting a single meaningful target word from the instruction, and the default BOW encoder ignores word order.
builds_on: UNREAL (auxiliary tasks: reward prediction, value replay)
compares_to: ablations with subsets of RP/VR/LP/tAE auxiliaries
